summary: A funded collar is not possible for CBA Board directors, Group Company Secretaries, Group Executives or their Associates: para 9 bans any transaction that limits the economic risk of their exposure to any vested Group Securities, and para 16(a) bans using Group Securities as security for margin lending or any other secured financing. For other Specified Persons (e.g. Executive General Managers, Subsidiary Board directors, Group Control Room staff), the hedge leg over vested shares free of any holding lock is not expressly banned, but the OTC options are Securities and entering them is a Trade, so it must be done in a Trading Window, with Pre-Clearance where designated on the Conflicts Hub (valid three business days), subject to the 30-day LIFO holding rule, and it must not involve CFDs, short selling or stock lending of Group Securities. The loan leg secured on the collared shares is prohibited for all Specified Persons, so at most an unsecured or unfunded collar is workable for that group, and exercise or settlement mechanics that execute outside a Trading Window are a further risk under para 11. Employees who are not Specified Persons face only the insider trading prohibition and whatever Pre-Clearance the unpublished Procedure imposes. The MAR overlay in para 18 adds an outright bar for the senior group on any Security that prices off a UK/EU-listed Group Security.

summary: A funded collar is possible under this policy, which is a short 2011 insider-trading document with no substantive prohibitions on hedging, derivatives, margin lending or secured financing. Both collar legs are PME Securities because the definition expressly captures equity swaps, hedges and exchange-traded or over-the-counter options, cash-settled or not, so entering, rolling, unwinding and settling the collar are each Dealings that require prior written notice of intention to the Company Secretary, a written confirmation of no Inside Information, and advice from the Company Secretary that there is no known reason to preclude the Dealing, with execution inside 7 days. Dealings must fall within one of the three 30-day Trading Windows after the full-year results, half-year results and AGM, outside the two four-week Blackout Periods and any ad hoc Blackout the Board or Chairman declares, and the Chairman may shorten a window or bar an individual; out-of-window execution needs the Chairman's (or for the Chairman, the Board's) approval on exceptional circumstances such as severe financial hardship, subject to any conditions including disclosure. The secured loan is not itself a Dealing and is not prohibited, but full details of any margin lending or other security arrangement affecting the shares must be reported in writing to the Company Secretary after the Dealing, and directors must also meet their notifiable interest obligations and their letter agreement with the company. The main residual risks are the narrow dealing calendar with no forced-sale carve-out, and the rules of the Pro Medicus Share and Option Plans, which are incorporated by reference and may impose hedging or encumbrance restrictions on plan shares that this policy does not.

summary: A funded collar is not possible for IAG Specified Persons, the population that includes the directors and executives a bank would target. Clause 34, added by the 30 November 2023 amendment, prohibits Specified Persons and their Closely Related Parties from using IAG Securities as collateral in any financial transaction, with margin lending and transfers into a margin account given only as examples, and no approver has power to waive it. The derivative legs alone are also constrained: instruments that limit economic risk are themselves IAG Securities, so entry, roll and unwind each require a Trading Consent Request approved by the Group General Counsel & Company Secretary (or, for Non-Executive Directors, the more senior approver route), inside one of the three roughly 20 business day Trading Windows, valid for only 5 business days, subject to the front page test whose refusal is final and confidential, and subject to the three-month short-term trading ban. Plan shares can never be hedged before vesting or while under a holding lock, so only fully vested unrestricted shares are candidates, and any price-triggered or conditional feature must be both placed and executed within a window. A collar could in principle be offered on an unsecured basis over vested unrestricted shares, and Directors, Employees and Contractors who are not Specified Persons are not caught by clauses 30 or 34 at all, but for the target population the funded structure is barred.

summary: A funded collar is not possible under this policy. Section 11.1 prohibits Directors, KMP and Employees from trading in any financial products issued or created over the Company's securities, which captures both the purchased put and the written call whether traded OTC or on exchange, with no clearance route, no exceptional-circumstances relief and no distinction by vesting state. summary: A funded collar is possible under this policy, and this is one of the more permissive ASX policies for the purpose. There is no hedging prohibition at all: products that limit the economic risk of holding SGH shares are simply defined as SGH securities, so the put and call legs are dealings that a designated employee may execute inside one of the three 30-working-day window periods following the half year results, annual results and AGM, or outside a window with prior written clearance from the approver named in the section 3 table. Margin lending is likewise expressly permitted with written clearance, which may be granted subject to conditions, and a disposal by a secured lender exercising its rights is carved out of the policy entirely provided the facility itself was cleared, which protects the bank on enforcement. The two hard constraints are that no Executive or designated staff member may deal in any financial product issued or created over or in respect of SGH securities during a blackout period, with no exceptional circumstances relief, and that clearance lapses after two business days, so the trade must be fully documented before approval is sought. summary: A funded collar is realistically achievable under this policy, which is markedly more permissive than most ASX policies on the financing leg. There is no prohibition on margin lending, secured financing, pledging or encumbering Lynas securities, granting security is not within the definition of Deal In Securities, and paragraph 8.1(6) expressly excludes from the policy a disposal resulting from a secured lender exercising its rights, so the bank's enforcement sale would not put the executive in breach even in a closed period. The derivative legs are the constraint: a put and call over Lynas shares are financial products created over the Company's securities and cannot be traded during prohibited periods (14.1), and since 7.3 makes every period a closed period except the three weeks following results, the AGM or a prospectus, entry, roll, unwind and settlement must each be timed into one of those narrow windows and preceded by written confirmation of no impediment from the Chairman (directors) or Secretary (employees). The 13.2 hedging ban reaches only employee options before vesting, so vested shares may be collared, but the undefined at all times ban on short-term trading in 13.1 argues for a long tenor and for clearing the structure explicitly. Out-of-window relief under 9.2 covers only a sale of securities, not derivative dealings, so no exceptional-circumstances route exists for an emergency unwind, and directors should expect the position to surface through immediate notification to the company secretary and an Appendix 3Y.

summary: A funded collar is close to workable at BlueScope but is defeated by the financing leg as ordinarily documented. The derivative legs are unusually accommodating: the policy names a 'cap or collar facility' and third party put and call options in the list of restricted trading rather than in a prohibition, so a Restricted Person may enter a collar over vested, unrestricted shares provided it is done inside one of the three trading windows (45 days after each of the half year and full year results, and 15 days after the AGM), after written notice to the Company Secretary, confirmation of no inside information and written clearance, which is valid for 10 trading days and revocable at any time. The loan leg is the problem: Restricted Persons must not enter into any new arrangement pledging BlueScope Steel securities as collateral for a loan or other agreement which could permit a sale without the holder's consent, with no clearance route and no exemption authority, and any resulting forced sale is a breach for which exceptions will expressly not be considered. The prohibition is conditional rather than absolute, so a structure in which the bank has no independent power of sale over the collared shares is the only route worth exploring. Two further constraints apply: nothing may be hedged while unvested or within a restriction period, and the nine month short-term trading ban means the collar tenor and the seasoning of the underlying shares must both exceed nine months.

summary: A funded collar is realistically achievable at WiseTech, which is one of the more permissive policies in the market. Hedging is banned only for plan securities that are unvested or subject to a holding lock or plan dealing restriction, so vested unrestricted shares, including shares bought on market, may be hedged; the derivative legs would be a dealing requiring only prior notification to the Company Secretary and the Chair for a Director (with a 5 business day window and a same-day post-trade confirmation), or approval on a Clearance to Trade Request Form for other Restricted Persons, answered typically within one business day. The funding leg is likewise available: the only financing rule is that a margin lending arrangement, or a transfer of shares into an existing margin loan account, needs approval under section 5.5, and the Company may impose conditions on that approval, notably about when shares may be sold to satisfy a margin call; there is no encumbrance ban, no vesting restriction on collateral and no financier disclosure obligation. Critically, section 6(e) treats a disposal resulting from a secured lender exercising its rights as an Excluded Dealing outside the short-term trading ban, the blackout periods and the notification and approval requirements, so a bank enforcement sale does not put the executive in breach. The practical conditions are that entry falls outside the 30 June and 31 December blackout periods and any Board-specified or Company-notified dealing ban, that the tenor and the seasoning of the underlying shares both exceed six months to avoid the short-term dealing rule, and that the structure is disclosed and cleared on a substance over form basis, since the Company can condition its approval on the enforcement mechanics of the loan.

However, section 5.2 flatly prohibits Restricted Persons from entering into margin lending arrangements in relation to the Company's securities, with no approval route, and the express substance over form principle means a bank facility secured on the collared shares with LVR or margin call mechanics is likely to be treated as such, so a funded structure would need to be demonstrably not a margin lending arrangement. Tenor is a further constraint: forward contracts are expressly given as an example of a prohibited short term dealing and buying and selling within 90 days is banned, so the collar should run well beyond 90 days. The loan leg is likewise an approval regime rather than a ban: section 5.3 requires approval for entering a margin lending arrangement over Netwealth securities, transferring shares into the lender's account and selling shares to meet a call, and the approver may impose conditions on when the collateral may be sold, while section 6(e) puts a secured lender's enforcement sale outside the blackout, approval and short-term trading rules entirely. The collar must be sized only to vested, unrestricted shares, because plan securities may never be hedged before vesting or while subject to a holding lock. The main traps are tenor and disclosure: forward contracts are given as an example of prohibited short-term dealing so the structure should run well beyond three months or be authorised by the NWL Board, and the arrangement must be entered in the personal Trading Register and disclosed in the annual declaration, with directors' and KMP interests published to the market where required.

summary: A funded collar is possible under this policy, but only over a narrow slice of shares and with an important gap in the documentation. summary: A funded collar is not available to a BOQ Designated Person, which includes every Director and member of Key Management Personnel. The obstacle is paragraph 31(b), a standalone prohibition on Designated Persons and their closely related parties dealing at any time in financial products over or in respect of Company Securities, where Financial Products is defined to include derivatives, options, forward contracts, swaps and contracts for difference created by third parties; unlike the remuneration hedging ban in 31(a) it is not limited to unvested or holding-locked shares, and a put option is expressly named as a prohibited arrangement. The financing leg, by contrast, is unusually accommodating: paragraph 26 bans only margin lending, paragraph 27 expressly states that the restriction does not extend to other funding arrangements where Company Securities may be included as security, and Appendix 1 item 6 lets a secured lender enforce at any time, including during a Prohibited Period, provided the facility is not a prohibited margin loan. The only route to a collar would be a written ruling from the General Counsel & Company Secretary that it is a 'type of dealing permitted by law or under this policy' within the closing words of paragraph 31(b), which is a genuine ambiguity but a thin basis for a bank to lend against, and no exemption power exists since the Appendix 2 exceptional circumstances relief reaches only paragraph 24 dealings and disposals. Even then the 30 day short term trading test, which expressly covers derivatives, and the Front Page Test would apply.

summary: A funded collar is not possible for Directors or Senior/Group Executives under this policy. Section 7.6 imposes an absolute, venue-neutral ban on hedging arrangements, dealing in derivatives, and contracts (including CFDs) intended to secure a profit or avoid a loss from price movements in Downer's securities, applying to all Directors, employees and contractors with no approval route, which squarely catches the OTC put and call legs of a collar. Even if the option legs could somehow be structured around this ban, section 7.7 separately and expressly prohibits Restricted Persons — Directors, Senior Executives, Executives and other notified staff, i.e. the bank's target clientele — from margin lending, securities lending, or granting any security interest, mortgage, charge, lien or encumbrance over Downer securities, barring the secured loan leg outright. Outside these express bans, an ordinary sale requires Company Secretary or Chairman approval outside the 28-day post-AGM/results open windows and is barred in Closed Periods, and a lender's forced close-out sale within six months of acquisition is separately deemed prohibited short-term trading. The Chairman (or Chairman of the Audit and Risk Committee) retains a narrow discretion to exempt a Closed Period dealing in exceptional circumstances, but never while undisclosed price-sensitive information is held, and this offers no relief from the hedging or margin-lending prohibitions. In short, both the derivative legs and the secured-financing leg of a collar are independently and expressly prohibited, with no carve-out for vested shares.

summary: A funded collar is possible under this policy, which is a short 2017 document that is silent on hedging, derivatives generally, margin lending, encumbrances and secured financing. Both derivative legs and the grant of security over the shares would be treated as proposed trades in Company securities requiring prior written notice to the Chairman and his written permission before execution, with written confirmation of the completed transaction back to the Chairman within 3 business days and, for a Director, a holdings report within one business day. Execution must avoid the closed periods, which run from 2 business days before each quarterly, half-year and full-year results announcement to the announcement itself and expressly extend to derivatives over the Company's securities. Tenor should exceed 30 days to stay clear of the short-term trading ban, and the policy offers the bank no forced-sale protection because it says nothing about lender enforcement in a closed period.

summary: A funded collar is possible under this policy, which is unusually accommodating: section 12 permits hedging arrangements that limit the economic risk of a security holding, and section 13 permits margin loans and other secured lending arrangements in relation to Company Securities, in each case subject to prior written clearance from the appropriate Approving Officer rather than being prohibited. summary: A funded collar is theoretically permitted but practically very hard under this policy, because both legs of the structure are routed to the same narrow gate. Dealing in derivatives, hedging arrangements and other arrangements limiting economic risk related to Megaport Securities, including put and call options and CFDs by name, require Written Clearance, and granting any form of security directly or indirectly over Megaport Securities to any third party including a margin lender also requires Written Clearance; neither is banned outright, and unvested and holding-locked securities are expressly within the security gate rather than excluded. The difficulty is that the Authorised Trading paragraph makes Written Clearance for speculative trading and for security arrangements available only where exceptional circumstances exist, illustrated by exceptional financial hardship, a court order or exceptional detriment to family affairs, and only where the trade is not for speculative gain and not likely to be seen by the public, press, other shareholders or ASX as unfair. A director would need sign-off from two directors (two non-executive directors or a non-executive director and the CEO or CFO for the Chair), must disclose volume and timing, must execute within 7 days of clearance, faces long Closed Periods running from 9 June and 10 December plus an AGM window and any Board-imposed Restricted Period, and must notify the Company Secretary within 2 days of each trade. The one clearly favourable feature for a bank is that a disposal of Megaport Securities by a secured lender under a loan agreement secured by those securities falls entirely outside the Policy, so enforcement is not a policy breach.

summary: A funded collar is not possible under this policy. ad_hoc_blackout_authority: The Fletcher Building Company Secretary (Deputy Company Secretary if unavailable) holds the discretion: 'the approval to trade is at the discretion of the Fletcher Building Company Secretary' and Schedule II is only a set of 'general guidelines on when approval will not be granted'. The event-driven No Trade Periods for capital structure changes and corporate activity are self-executing and by their nature undisclosed, and refusals are confidential because 'In declining any approval to trade, no reasons need be given.'
exemption_authority: No formal exemption or waiver power. The Company Secretary has an unfettered discretion to grant or refuse consent to trade ('the approval to trade is at the discretion of the Fletcher Building Company Secretary'), and Schedule II is expressed as guidance only, so the Company Secretary can in principle consent during a listed No Trade Period. The clause 6 ban on limiting the economic risk of equity incentive remuneration is absolute and has no waiver route. The Board approves the Policy.
external_documents: Fletcher Building Code of Conduct (incorporated into the terms of employment) | Fletcher Building Corporate Governance practices, approved by the board annually | Company employee share scheme rules | Executive Long-Term Share Scheme (and similar legacy schemes) rules
jurisdiction_overlays: New Zealand Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 insider trading regime is the primary legal overlay, not the Corporations Act | Dual listed NZX (FBU) and ASX (FBU); designated persons must make securities trading disclosures to both NZX and ASX | New Zealand Takeovers Code (specific insider trading exemption relied on for the takeover carve-out) | Policy expressly contemplates conduct outside New Zealand: 'even conduct that occurs entirely outside of New Zealand can also be subject to New Zealand's insider trading legislation'
summary: A funded collar over fully vested, unrestricted Fletcher Building shares is achievable, and this is one of the more permissive policies of its kind. The Policy is silent on margin lending, secured financing, charges and forced sales, so the loan leg secured on the collared shares is not prohibited; the put and call legs are caught only as a 'trade' under paragraph 1.1, which expressly includes trading in derivatives over or relating to Fletcher Building securities with no venue limit. The conditions are prior written notification to and consent from the Company Secretary using the prescribed form (which contemplates an off-market trade), execution within the 10 trading day validity, no material information at execution, and timing outside the 1 July and 1 January No Trade Periods and any undisclosed capital-raising or corporate-activity blackout. The decisive constraint is clause 6: any employee offered equity based incentive remuneration is absolutely prohibited, with no consent route, from any transaction limiting the economic risk of that incentive remuneration, so the collar must be confined to shares whose incentive has been 'achieved' - vested with full and unrestricted title transferred - and must not reach awards still subject to performance hurdles or restriction. Consent is discretionary and may be refused without reasons, so neither entry nor any later roll or unwind can be treated as assured.

summary: A funded collar is not possible under this policy, although the unfunded hedge legs could be. Restricted Persons (directors, the Managing Director, Leadership Team and other designated staff) may enter a purchased put and written call over vested, unrestricted shares as a dealing requiring prior notification and consent from the Company Secretary (Chairman of the Board if the person is a Director or the size exceeds 100,000 shares/options), executed within 10 trading days, outside the half-year and full-year black-out periods, and only while not in possession of Inside Information; the express hedging ban applies only to unvested 'at-risk' remuneration. However, the policy separately and unconditionally prohibits employees from 'entering into margin lending and other secured financing arrangements' in respect of Spark New Zealand Restricted Securities, with no tier carve-out, security-state distinction or exemption authority, so the loan leg secured on the collared shares cannot be put in place. Consent for the derivative legs is discretionary, may be refused without reasons, and lapses automatically if Inside Information arises before execution. General employees outside the Restricted Persons/Directors tiers face no consent regime at all beyond the fundamental Inside Information prohibition, but are equally bound by the secured financing ban.

Within Part 3, the Notification Officer (or the Chair of the Board/Audit Committee for other exceptional circumstances) may permit dealing during a Closed Period only for defined exceptional circumstances, and any such approval 'must be obtained in advance, cannot be given after the event and will be final and binding.'

summary: A funded collar is not possible under this policy for Key Management Personnel or their Associates. Paragraph 4.1 imposes an absolute, carve-out-free ban on dealing 'at any time' in options, warrants, futures or other financial products issued over NHF Securities by third parties such as banks, which catches both the purchased put and written call legs of an OTC collar; paragraph 4.2 separately names 'a put option on incentive remuneration' as a prohibited hedging arrangement and more broadly bans transactions limiting the economic risk of a KMP's security holding. The loan leg is not entirely closed off: margin loans over NHF Securities are prohibited outright, but 'other secured financial arrangements' over NHF Securities are expressly permitted subject to Board approval, so a loan secured on the shares could in principle be approved on its own. A secured lender's enforcement sale, if it ever occurred, is a Schedule 4 excluded dealing outside the Closed Period/notification regime, though always subject to the insider trading ban. Because the option components have no approval or exceptional-circumstances route anywhere in the policy, the collar as a whole cannot be implemented notwithstanding the more permissive secured-financing provision.

external_documents: Platinum Investment Management Limited's Business Rules of Conduct (personal trading rules)
summary: A funded collar's option legs are prohibited under this policy: section C(d) bars Covered Persons from entering into transactions in derivative instruments or other products associated with L1G Securities that operate to limit the economic risk of their holding, which squarely catches a purchased put and written call regardless of vesting state, and there is no clearance or exemption route for this prohibition (the Company Secretary's discretionary exemption applies only to breaches of the Closed Trading Period and short-term trading rules). By contrast, the policy is entirely silent on margin lending, secured financing and encumbrance of L1G Securities, so a loan secured on the collared shares is not itself restricted. Ordinary, non-hedging dealing in L1G Securities (including derivatives) by Covered Persons is permitted with one-Business-Day pre-clearance (route depending on the L1 Group entity involved), outside Closed Trading Periods and the six-month short-term trading window, and only while not aware of inside information. Because the hedging prohibition has no carve-out anywhere in the policy, a bank-funded collar cannot be implemented notwithstanding the complete absence of any restriction on the loan leg.

ad_hoc_blackout_authority: The Board may restrict Directors, GLT members and Specified Managers from dealing during any other period if, in its opinion, information available to them could affect the price or value of Securities (e.g. around a market-sensitive announcement); not stated to be confidential, though a refused or revoked approval must be kept confidential.

exemption_authority: Only for dealing during a prohibited period (section 3.1): the Chair of Metcash Limited (Directors/GLT), the Chair of the Audit, Risk and Compliance Committee (for the Chair's own dealings) or the Group CEO (Specified Managers) may grant approval only in exceptional circumstances (severe financial hardship, court order/undertaking or family settlement) and only if the applicant holds no inside information. The Approver need not give reasons, may impose conditions, and may revoke approval at any time without reason; any refusal or revocation must be kept confidential. No exemption authority is stated for the section 6.1 hedging/derivative ban.
summary: A funded collar over fully vested, unrestricted Metcash shares appears largely unrestricted by this policy: 'Securities' is defined narrowly as Metcash's own shares, options, notes, performance rights and debentures, so a bank-written OTC put and call are not 'Securities' and fall outside the Closed Period, approval and short-term dealing rules; the only hedging/derivative prohibition (section 6.1) is expressly confined to Securities that are unvested or still subject to a holding lock under an incentive plan. The loan leg is also workable: Directors and GLT members who finance acquisitions of Securities by margin call loans need only advise the Company Secretary for a register (with the Chair told of any lender intention to sell) rather than seek approval, though it is unclear whether this notification duty extends to a loan secured on already-vested shares rather than financing a purchase, and it does not extend to Specified Management at all. If the shares remain subject to a holding lock, or dealing occurs within a Closed Period (1 October to half-year results; 1 April to full-year results) or another Board-specified restricted period, prior written approval from the Chair (or the Group CEO for Specified Managers) is required, and is discretionary, conditional and revocable without reason. A secured lender's enforcement sale is expressly excluded from the short-term dealing and Closed Period rules. Overall, once shares are vested and unrestricted, this policy permits a funded collar with only light-touch disclosure, making it comparatively more accommodating than policies with a broader dealing/derivatives definition.

title: Securities Trading Policy

summary: A funded collar over vested Zip shares is structurally available but fully discretionary. Both the derivative legs (put and call, caught as a hedging arrangement under clause 8.1) and the secured loan (clause 8.2) require prior written approval from an Approving Officer (the Chairperson for Directors/Officers/GET, or the Company Secretary/CFO/Executive Director for other Zip Personnel), executed outside the four annual Prohibited Periods and any confidential Board-imposed blackout, and while the executive holds no inside information. Hedging of unvested entitlements under an equity-based remuneration scheme is absolutely prohibited by clause 7.1 with no approval route, so the collar must be confined to shares that have already vested. Approval, once granted, is valid for only 7 business days and may be refused or revoked at the Approving Officer's absolute and unreviewable discretion, kept confidential if declined, so timing and durability are real execution risks. Family trusts or entities controlled by the executive do not escape these requirements, as they are themselves defined as Zip Personnel.

summary: A funded collar appears achievable under this Policy, which is unusually permissive: there is no hedging-specific prohibition at all, and both encumbering the shares (the loan leg) and entering the derivative legs as ordinary 'trading' are approvable with prior written approval, even inside a Closed Period in exceptional circumstances (hardship, court order or Board discretion) for the encumbrance. Outside Closed Periods, standard prior written approval from the Chair, CEO or Managing Director (or the Audit Committee Chair if the applicant is the Chair) is required, automatically lapses if the person acquires Inside Information or a Closed Period begins, and must be exercised within its stated time limit, so execution should be timed to an open window. A secured lender's enforcement sale on default or margin call is expressly excluded from the Closed Period ban and needs no fresh approval, which reduces the bank's counterparty risk on enforcement. As a Canadian-incorporated dual-listed entity, a Reporting Insider entering the collar will likely also need to file a SEDI report on the resulting 'related financial instrument' within about five days, a disclosure duty separate from the ASX-side clearance process. Directors additionally must report the transaction to the Corporate Secretary within 2 business days for onward 5-business-day ASX disclosure.

summary: A funded collar is plausibly achievable, and on unusually favourable terms if the narrow definitions are read literally. 'Company Securities' and 'deal' are defined narrowly (the Company's own shares/debentures/options, and subscribing, purchasing, selling or agreeing to do so), so the OTC put and call legs of a collar with a bank may not themselves be caught by the Policy's Company Secretary approval process or Blackout Periods at all, though this reading should be confirmed given the general principles in clause 6.1. The loan leg is expressly not banned: normal documented margin lending or loan facilities from banks or lending institutions are carved out of the broker-credit prohibition, though the 'offered to the general public' qualifier leaves some doubt for a bespoke bilateral facility. Directors must separately notify ASX within 5 business days of entering any contract conferring a right to call for or deliver Company shares, which squarely covers an option-based collar, and within 14 days of any change in relevant interest. Any actual sale or transfer of the underlying shares (e.g. on settlement) is a 'deal' requiring prior notification to, and subsequent written confirmation with, the Company Secretary, must avoid the fixed half-year and monthly NTA Blackout Periods (absent exceptional-circumstances consent), and should not be structured to look like short-term trading within 12 months of acquisition.

title: Securities Dealing Policy

For blackout-period dealing (5.3) and short-term dealing (6.1), the CEO (Senior Executives/Nominated Employees/Employees), the Chair of the Board (Directors), or the Chair of the Audit and Risk Committee (the Chair) may approve in their sole discretion where exceptional circumstances (severe financial hardship or court order) are evidenced.
summary: A funded collar is not possible under this Policy for any tier. Hedging of the Company's securities - which a purchased put and written call over vested shares squarely constitutes - is banned outright by clause 6.3 with no exceptions process anywhere in the Policy. Separately, clause 6.2 bans any dealing connected with a margin lending arrangement, including entering the arrangement, transferring shares into it, and selling to meet a call, again with no approval route, and the Company's stated substance-over-form approach (section 10) means a differently-labelled but functionally equivalent share-secured loan is unlikely to escape that ban. The only relief mechanisms in the Policy - the exceptional-circumstances approval for blackout-period dealing and for short-term dealing, and the equity-plan/DRP/takeover/non-discretionary-plan exclusions - apply to different, unrelated restrictions (windows, short-term trading) and do not extend to either the hedging or the margin lending prohibition. A secured lender's own enforcement sale on default is excused from blackout and approval requirements, but that does not make entry into the loan itself lawful under the Policy.

summary: A funded collar over vested, unrestricted Chorus shares appears achievable. The Policy's only hedging-specific prohibition is expressly limited to unvested 'at-risk' remuneration, so hedging vested shares is treated as an ordinary dealing in a Chorus Restricted Security (a category that expressly includes derivatives): for a Restricted Person this needs prior written consent from the General Counsel and Company Secretary (plus Chairman approval if the person is a Director or the trade exceeds 100,000 shares/options), consent lasting 10 trading days and lapsing automatically if Inside Information arises, executed outside the two annual results black-out periods (or any ad hoc GC&CS-declared period) absent severe hardship or a court order; for other Chorus Personnel, only the fundamental no-dealing-on-Inside-Information rule applies, with no consent process at all. The Policy is entirely silent on margin lending, secured financing and encumbrance, so the loan leg of the collar is not expressly addressed either way, and the Bank should confirm whether pledging the shares or transferring them to a collateral agent is treated as 'dealing' requiring the same consent, given the Policy's example that transferring shares to a trust does require consent. As a dual NZX/ASX-listed issuer, the Policy applies to dealings anywhere in the world, so an offshore-booked collar is not outside its scope.

title: Share Trading Policy (Section 5 of the Corporate Governance Charter)
tiers: Restricted Persons | Associated Parties
ad_hoc_blackout_authority: The Company may from time to time designate further prohibited periods; separately the Board has an absolute discretion to place an embargo on Restricted Persons and/or associated parties trading at any time. Confidentiality of such embargoes is not addressed.

summary: A funded collar is not possible in the form the bank typically offers, because clause 5.10 imposes an absolute, clearance-free ban on any 'hedging arrangement' or transaction in financial products that limits the economic risk of holding L1 Long Short Fund shares, which squarely catches an OTC purchased put and written call; there is no exemption authority for this ban. The financing leg is more workable: margin lending or similar secured financing is not prohibited but requires the Company's prior written consent (via the Chairperson and Company Secretary), and the Company can impose conditions, including on when a lender may sell to meet a margin call. Even if the derivative ban were somehow structured around, ordinary share dealing (including any sale on unwind) requires prior notification to the Company Secretary and is barred during the four annual blackout periods (5 business days around dividend/capital management announcements, half-year results, full-year results and the AGM) and during any Board-imposed embargo, with only a narrow sale-only hardship exception available from the Chairperson. Because there is no employee equity incentive scheme, there is no unvested/vested distinction; the shares in question would be ordinary vested holdings throughout. Overall, the bank could not lawfully write the derivative legs of a collar for a Restricted Person or their associates under this policy as currently drafted.

summary: For a PDMR (director or senior executive with regular access to Inside Information), a funded collar with a bank is not possible: section 5 imposes an absolute, permanent, clearance-free prohibition on Dealing in any financial product created over or in respect of Company Securities (expressly including hedge arrangements) and on margin lending or similar secured arrangements, with no exception in Schedules 1 or 2. For other Personnel, both legs are only 'Dealings' under the broad definitions (which expressly cover derivatives, agreements to deal, and using shares as security for a loan), so a collar is structurally possible subject to prior written clearance from the Approving Officer (5 Business Day validity, 3 Business Day response), post-trade notification to the Company Secretary within 1 Business Day, and execution outside the frequent Closed Periods (which run from the start of each quarter/half-year/year until results are published, plus event-driven blackouts). Routing a PDMR's collar through a family member or trust (a PCA) is legally uncertain, since the absolute section 5 ban is not among the sections expressly extended to PCAs, but the PDMR's overriding duty to prevent PCA breaches makes this an unreliable workaround rather than a safe structuring route. No exemption authority exists for the section 5 ban; the only discretionary relief (Exceptional Circumstances) is limited to a sale-only clearance during a Closed Period and would not authorise a collar's derivative or loan legs in any event.

There is no hardship, court-order or other discretionary waiver from the black-out periods or the derivatives ban; only the fixed exceptions in clause 3.6 (managed portfolios, dividend reinvestment plans, option exercise) apply, and the Board's power under 3.5(c) is only to add further blackout periods, not to grant relief from them.

summary: A funded collar is not possible under this policy for any Mesoblast Personnel or their Connected Persons. Clause 3.3 imposes an absolute, unconditional and undefined ban on trading in 'the Company's derivatives', with no clearance mechanism, no exception in clause 3.6, no vesting distinction, and no discretionary waiver authority anywhere in the document, so the purchased put and written call legs of an OTC collar are prohibited outright regardless of whether the shares are vested. This ban extends to a Designated Person's spouse, minor children, nominee or investment manager, family trust, or family-controlled company, so routing the derivative through an associate does not avoid it. By contrast, the loan leg is entirely unaddressed: the policy contains no provision on margin lending, encumbrance or secured financing, so a standalone secured loan (without the derivative overlay) would not itself breach this policy. Because the collar's option legs are banned, the structure as a whole cannot be implemented, and any attempt to acquire the securities or deal via a trust or company while in possession of inside information would separately risk an insider trading contravention. The document is dated 2013 with no evidence of subsequent amendment, so its current force should be confirmed before relying on it.

Whether this discretion can extend to override the separate 'at any time' bans on protection arrangements and security-granting/margin lending over unvested or holding-locked securities (3.5(a), 3.6(a)) is untested, since those bans are not framed as prohibitions on 'Dealing' (the defined term used in 4.3).

summary: A funded collar is workable under this policy, but only once the underlying OBM shares have fully vested and any holding lock has lifted: over unvested or holding-locked shares, both the derivative legs (a 'protection arrangement' under 3.5, expressly including hedging and short selling) and the loan's security (3.6) are banned at any time with no exception. Once the shares are vested and unrestricted, both legs become merely approval-gated: an OBM Person or their Connected Person may enter into the protection arrangement and grant security over the shares (to secure their own or even a third party's obligation, covering the bank loan) with prior written approval from the Authorising Officer (5 trading days' validity, revocable, refusal confidential but not final in the sense that a fresh request can always be made). Execution must also avoid the quarterly, half-year and full-year Blackout Periods (and any additional period set by the Board or Managing Director) unless the Authorising Officer grants an exceptional-circumstances approval for hardship or a court order. Distinctively, OBM's policy expressly carves out a secured lender's enforcement sale on default from the Policy altogether, including during a Blackout Period, provided the original security grant was itself approved, which meaningfully de-risks the bank's enforcement rights. Key Management Personnel must separately notify the Company Secretary of every Dealing, including exempt ones, within two business days for ASIC/ASX reporting.

title: Securities Trading Policy

summary: For Key Management Personnel, a funded collar is not possible: section 3.2(b) permanently and unconditionally bans using Company securities as collateral in any financial transaction (including margin lending), with no vesting distinction, no clearance route and no exclusion, so the secured loan leg cannot be implemented even though the derivative legs would become clearance-gated once the shares vest and any holding lock lifts. For Directors and Restricted Employees who are not KMP, the position is more favourable: the section 3.2(a) ban on risk-limiting transactions applies only while the shares are unvested or holding-locked, and once vested and unrestricted, both a put and a call are simply 'securities' (the definition expressly includes derivatives and contracts for difference) requiring ordinary prior written clearance, to be executed within 2 business days and outside Closed Periods. Secured financing is not expressly regulated for non-KMP personnel at all, and a lender's enforcement sale on default is expressly excluded from the Closed Period, clearance and short-term trading rules, which supports the bank's ability to rely on its security. Ordinary employees who are neither Directors, Restricted Employees nor KMP face only the general insider-trading prohibition and the unvested/holding-locked derivatives ban, with no formal clearance system for other dealings. Overall, a funded collar over fully vested, unrestricted shares held by a non-KMP Director or employee appears structurally achievable subject to timely clearance and window management, but is squarely blocked for any KMP.

summary: A funded collar over vested, unrestricted shares appears workable for Designated Persons (directors, ELT, the Company Secretary and other notified persons) subject to prior written approval from the applicable Approval Officer, confined to an open Trading Window, and executed within 5 business days of approval. Hedging is only expressly banned while shares are unvested or subject to a plan holding lock; once vested and unrestricted, entering into the put/call is an ordinary dealing requiring clearance rather than being prohibited outright. The Policy's only financing restriction bans 'margin lending arrangements' and transfers into an 'existing margin loan account', which is narrower than a full secured-financing ban, so a bespoke pledge-secured loan not structured as a margin loan is not expressly caught, though this should be confirmed given the Policy's substance-over-form approach. Usefully, a disposal resulting from a secured lender exercising its rights is an Excluded Dealing, exempt from both the short-term dealing ban and the Trading Window restriction, so the bank's enforcement sale is not blocked by a closed window. Residual risks are the ban on 'other short term dealings (for example, forward contracts)', which could catch a short-tenor collar, and the Approval Officer's unfettered, confidential discretion to refuse or revoke clearance under the Front Page Test.

summary: A funded collar over vested, unrestricted Genesis Energy shares appears achievable for Restricted Persons (directors, the Chief Executive and senior managers), subject to obtaining written pre-approval for the transaction -- from the Chief Executive, or the Chairman of the Board for Director/Chief Executive requests -- valid for 10 trading days (2 trading days if granted during a Blackout Period) and automatically withdrawn if Material Information comes to light. The Policy's only anti-hedging rule (the 'Associated Product' restriction) is framed around a person's unvested entitlement under an equity-based remuneration scheme, not securities already vested and held, so hedging of vested shares is not expressly banned on its wording, though this should be confirmed. Notably, the Policy contains no provision at all on margin lending, secured financing, encumbrance or a secured lender's enforcement rights, so the loan leg of the collar is neither prohibited nor subject to any notification duty under this document, though the silence and any NZ financial markets law overlay should be checked separately. Both the put/call derivatives and any monetisation fall within 'Securities'/'Trading' by definition (Securities expressly include options and derivatives), so they are subject to the same pre-approval and Blackout Period restrictions as an ordinary share trade, with post-trade details reported to the General Counsel and Company Secretary. The main residual constraints are the short-term trading discouragement (buying and selling within 3 months needs prior approval) and the Blackout Periods around each set of results and any prospectus, during which dealing needs exceptional-circumstances approval.

summary: A funded collar is not available to Designated Persons (the Chair, all directors including the Managing Director/CEO, and the MD/CEO's direct reports) under this Policy: creating any security interest or other financial interest, or entering a margin loan, over BWP securities is an express, unwaivable 'Prohibited Dealing' for which 'Board approval cannot be granted', and hedging any element of remuneration still subject to disposal restrictions is separately and equally unwaivable. Once shares vest and any disposal restriction lifts, hedging is not itself banned and, together with an OTC put/call and any monetisation, is an ordinary Dealing (hedges and derivatives are expressly named) requiring prior written authorisation from the Managing Director/CEO (or the Chair for the MD/CEO's own dealing, or the independent chair of the Audit and Risk Committee for the Chair's own dealing), confined outside Blackout Periods and lapsing after 5 business days for an off-market transaction. For BWP Personnel who are not Designated Persons, none of the 7.2 prohibitions apply -- margin loans, security interests and hedges are all merely Dealings subject only to the insider trading rules and the Front Page Test, so a funded collar would in principle be workable for that group, though they are unlikely to be the bank's target clients. Because the security-interest ban is absolute for Designated Persons, the Policy provides no secured-lender enforcement carve-out and no financing disclosure regime for that tier. Overall, the funded collar as a whole is blocked for the directors and executives the bank is targeting, and only an unfunded, hedge-only structure could be contemplated for them, subject to authorisation.

summary: A funded collar is not available under this Policy for any Employee or Designated Officer, at any vesting stage: clause 14 imposes a blanket, unconditional ban on entering into transactions -- expressly including hedging arrangements, margin loans and share lending arrangements, and by its 'includes, but is not limited to' wording likely any other risk-limiting or secured financing arrangement -- that operate to limit the economic risk of holding any Company security or any vested or unvested equity-remuneration entitlement. No clearance, exemption or exceptional-circumstances route in the Policy reaches this prohibition; the exceptional-circumstances discretion in clause 10 only relieves the Blackout Period and Executive Trading Window timing restrictions on ordinary dealing, not the clause 14 ban. Outside of a collar structure, an outright sale or purchase of vested shares by a Designated Officer requires prior written clearance from the Approving Officer (the Managing Director/CEO, or the chairperson of the Audit Committee for other directors), valid for only 14 days, and is barred altogether during quarterly Blackout Periods and while in possession of inside information; ordinary Employees face no clearance requirement but the same Blackout Period and insider trading restrictions apply. Because margin loans and share lending are outright prohibitions rather than merely regulated activities, the Policy contains no secured-lender enforcement carve-out and no financing disclosure regime. In short, the bank's funded collar cannot be offered to directors or executives of this company under the current Policy.

summary: A funded OTC collar is workable once the GYG shares have vested and are free of any holding lock: both the put/call structure (a 'protection arrangement' under 9.2, since it limits economic risk and could profit from a price fall) and the loan secured on the shares (9.3) are permitted with prior consent from the Authorising Officer, taken outside Blackout Periods and while not in possession of Inside Information. Both legs are prohibited outright, with no consent route, while the shares remain unvested or subject to a holding lock. Consent is granted by the Chair of the Board or Audit & Risk Committee chair for directors and senior KMP, and by the Company Secretary or General Counsel for other staff, though the policy's own section headings leave some doubt as to whether non-Director/Senior-Management participants can access this route. A useful feature for the bank is the express carve-out permitting a secured lender's enforcement sale 'at any time', including during a Blackout Period, so default enforcement against the collared shares would not itself breach the policy. There is no minimum shareholding requirement and no defined short-term holding period beyond a general, undated ban on short-term or speculative trading, and the only exemption authority is the Board's case-by-case discretion for hardship or court orders.

summary: A funded OTC collar is achievable over vested, unrestricted Lovisa shares: hedging is banned outright before vesting and while subject to a holding lock, but hedging vested, unrestricted shares is expressly permitted once processed as an ordinary dealing under clause 3.3. For directors and senior executives that means 48-hour advance notice during the four-week trading windows or prior written approval from the Chair/CEO outside them, executed within 2 business days and confirmed to the Company Secretary; for other Relevant Persons it is simply notified to the Company Secretary within 2 business days after dealing. The loan leg is only addressed as a 'margin lending arrangement', but directors and senior executives must obtain approval for it 'irrespective of any trading window', and the Company may condition that approval, including around margin-call sale triggers; a secured lender's enforcement sale is excluded from the ordinary dealing rules only 'subject to' that approval requirement. Entry, renewal or close-out cannot occur while the executive holds inside information, must avoid a 3-month short-term dealing pattern, and the Company may publicly disclose the fact and nature of the hedge. summary: A funded OTC collar is achievable under Tasmea's policy: its own definition of 'Derivatives' expressly includes 'collars', and while use of Derivatives is banned outright over unvested equity and vested securities still subject to a Holding Lock, it is expressly permitted over vested, unrestricted holdings with the prior written approval of the Chairperson (or the Board, if the Chairperson is the trader). The loan leg is separately regulated as a 'margin lending arrangement' (a term defined broadly enough to cover any borrowing secured on existing shares) and, for Key Management Personnel, requires tiered written approval; the Board only introduced this KMP margin-lending approval regime in August 2025 specifically to give the Founders financing flexibility. Both approvals must be obtained outside Black-out Periods, require the person not to hold Inside Information, and the Company may disclose the arrangement to the ASX. It is unclear whether the section 6.2 derivatives-approval requirement extends to employees, consultants or contractors who are not Designated Persons, since that section (unlike the surrounding ones) is not expressly limited to Designated Persons; the conservative reading is that Chairperson approval should be sought regardless of tier. Funding Arrangements that would limit risk exposure on remuneration that is unvested, or vested but still restricted, are banned outright, so the collar and its loan can only reference fully vested, unrestricted shares. Once approved, a lender's enforcement sale under the arrangement is an Excluded Dealing not subject to Blackout Period restrictions, but that protection depends on the Funding Arrangement having been properly Board-approved beforehand; the Restricted Person must also keep the Company Secretary informed of relevant changes in circumstances, and market disclosure of key terms is required if the arrangement covers 5% or more of the Company's securities. Section 8.3(b) imposes a standalone, unconditional ban on dealing 'at any time' in financial products associated with the Company's securities (expressly including derivatives and CFDs), subject only to permitted dealings in section 7, none of which covers entering an OTC put and call with a bank; this is an outright prohibition rather than a clearance gate, and it applies regardless of vesting state. The loan leg is more favourable: only 'margin lending arrangements' are banned (8.1), and the policy expressly states this does not extend to other secured funding arrangements over the Company's securities, with a secured lender's enforcement sale carved out as a Permitted Dealing available at any time. However, because the derivative overlay is banned outright, the favourable treatment of the secured loan is moot, and a funded collar cannot be implemented while this policy stands.

A secured (non-margin) lender's enforcement sale on default is excluded from the blackout-period restriction, supporting the bank's ability to enforce outside a trading window, but this carve-out does not extend to margin lending arrangements, so the facility should be documented and characterised as a non-margin secured loan. Because the funded structure inherently requires pledging the shares as collateral, a funded collar with a bank is not possible under this policy regardless of vesting state or timing; an unfunded collar (derivatives only, no security granted) would face no express bar but its treatment as a 'dealing' is untested and should be confirmed with the Company Secretary.

The loan leg is only conditionally restricted: a margin loan or other secured financing arrangement over Company Securities requires the Chairman's (or delegate's) prior approval, or the Board's if the Restricted Person is the Chairman, and once approved, a lender's subsequent enforcement sale is expressly excepted from the blackout-period restriction. Even setting the hedging ban aside, any derivative dealing (Securities is defined to include options and other derivatives) needs prior notification and Company Secretary/Chairman confirmation, cannot occur during the annual or half-year blackout periods, and is discouraged if the position is held six months or less. Closely Connected Persons (spouse, minor children, family trust or company) are bound by the same restrictions, so the structure cannot be routed around the hedging ban through them. Overall, the secured loan could in principle be approved but the put and call legs cannot, making a funded collar with a bank unavailable to Restricted Persons as drafted.

Strikingly, the policy contains no provision at all on margin lending, security interests or secured financing, so the loan leg secured against the collared shares is not addressed, restricted or conditioned by this Share Trading Policy. Non-Designated Beach People face a lighter regime of manager notification rather than approval for the same dealings. Overall, the derivative legs are approvable once shares are vested and unlocked and the loan is simply outside this policy's scope, but the undefined short-term dealing prohibition and the confidential ad hoc blackout power both create execution-timing risk for the bank.

summary: A funded collar is not achievable for Reporting Insiders or Designated Insiders (directors, KMP, and other designated officers/employees, together with their designated family members and closely connected persons) under this policy. The Anti-Hedging Restrictions impose an absolute, unconditional ban on 'transactions in derivatives in respect of Company Securities (such as put and call options), or any other hedging or equity monetization transaction ... (such as collars or forward sales contracts)' — collars are named verbatim — and unlike every other restriction in the policy (blackout-period trading, margin lending, short-term dealing/short selling), there is no approval, pre-clearance or exceptional-circumstances route that can lift it. The loan leg is only conditionally restricted: a margin loan or other secured financing arrangement over Company Securities requires prior approval of the General Counsel and Corporate Secretary and the Executive Chairman (or, for the Executive Chairman himself, the Lead Director), but this approval cannot cure the absolute ban on the derivative legs. Reporting Insiders and Designated Insiders may otherwise trade only within the open window beginning the third business day after quarterly, half-yearly or annual results and ending at the close of the following financial quarter, subject to written pre-clearance valid for five trading days and any discretionary blackout period imposed by the General Counsel and Corporate Secretary. Directors, officers and employees outside these two tiers face only the general insider trading prohibition, but they are also the population unlikely to hold the vested incentive equity a collar would be written over.

The document usefully exempts a secured lender's forced sale on default from the Blackout/dealing restrictions, so the bank's enforcement remedy is not itself blocked, though the executive must still notify the Authorising Officer. Tenor and structuring should avoid characterisation as 'short-term or speculative trading', which is banned outright with no defined holding period. Overall: workable over vested unrestricted shares with prior consent at each stage, but entirely blocked while shares remain unvested or holding-locked.

The loan leg is a Secured Lending Arrangement, permitted with the Responsible Person's (Chairman/ARC Chairman) prior written approval at any time for Global Leadership Team and Finance Team members, or via the same clause 7 route for other covered persons dealing under one, and carries ongoing disclosure of loan size, LVR and trigger points; that approval is revocable before completion and any approved terms may be publicly disclosed by the Company. A lender's forced sale on a margin call is an exempt dealing not requiring fresh clearance, but the Company expects GLT/Finance Team members to avoid needing one at all. Hedging of unvested equity incentive holdings needs separate Chairman consent under clause 6.8, and unwinding a large enough position (over 2% of issued capital in six months) needs additional Chairman/Board approval on timing and disclosure. The derivative legs fare better - the Derivatives definition expressly names 'collars' as a captured instrument, and their use is banned outright only over unvested or holding-locked shares (6.2(a)); over vested, unrestricted shares, derivatives are expressly permitted (6.2(b)) subject to the standard prior written approval of the relevant Approving Officer, a 5 business day clearance validity, avoidance of Black-out Periods, and post-trade notification to the Company Secretary within 5 business days. Because the financing leg is categorically prohibited with no clearance mechanism, a bank cannot lawfully take security over a Designated Person's Company Securities to fund the structure, even though the put and call could otherwise be cleared. The only partial relief is a narrow, Chair-approved Disposal Consent for disposals/transfers (not acquisitions or financing) during a Black-out Period in cases of genuine hardship or court order.

A lender's forced sale on default is an Excluded Trade requiring no fresh approval. Overall: workable with Board approval for the financing leg and Chairman approval for each derivative leg and any large unwind, and there is no vesting-state carve-out to navigate.

The loan leg is the key obstacle: clause 3.4 bans 'margin lending arrangements' using Company securities as security, and while a bespoke bank loan secured on the collared shares may not be a literal margin loan, the Policy's forced-sale exclusion (available only 'subject to paragraph 3.4') suggests secured lending over Company securities generally is not intended to be permitted, so structuring and approval risk falls on the loan. No minimum shareholding requirement or standing financing-disclosure obligation is stated, but the Company may separately disclose the hedge's existence in its annual report or to ASX, and each dealing must be confirmed to the Company Secretary within 2 business days. Tenor should exceed three months given the short-term dealing prohibition. The put/call derivative legs are 'securities'/'dealing' under the broad definitions (any derivatives, including options, and any agreement to acquire or dispose) and so require only a written pre-dealing notice to the Company Secretary (or, for the CEO, initial notice to the Chairman), completion within 14 days of the notice being received, and execution within a window period (six weeks after half-year or full-year results, or a rights trading period) or under a Designated Officer's exceptional-circumstances approval, never while holding inside information. A standard representation on the dealing forms states an intention not to sell newly purchased securities within 6 months, but this does not constrain hedging or encumbering already-held vested shares. If the bank needs to force a sale on default and that falls within a Closed Period, the Board must exercise its clause 4.1(f) discretion to permit it. Overall verdict: a funded collar is achievable with routine notice-based clearance in a window period, and the loan leg is not itself prohibited, making this one of the more collar-friendly policies, subject to checking the executive's own employee share plan or shareholder agreement for a stricter overriding term.

Critically for the loan leg, clause 9 requires the Designated Officer's (the Chairman's, or the Company Secretary's if the executive is the Chairman) prior written consent before granting a lender rights over the collared shares -- an express gate, not a prohibition. Any dealing must also avoid the two annual Blackout Periods (31 December to half-year results; 30 June to full-year results) and any confidential ad hoc restriction, and can never proceed while the person holds inside information, which overrides any approval already granted. Outside those windows, only an exceptional-circumstances approval from the Company Secretary or Chairman (for severe hardship, a court order, or a circumstance the Chairman or Audit & Compliance Chair deems exceptional) permits a disposal during a Blackout Period. Overall verdict: the put/call collar structure itself is workable with notification outside Blackout Periods, but the bank's loan secured on the collared shares is expressly and unconditionally prohibited for Designated Persons, making a standard funded collar not achievable without restructuring the financing so that no security is taken over Orora shares.

Hedging of unvested securities, or vested securities still subject to a plan holding lock, is an absolute, unconditional ban for every tier, so the collar cannot attach to those shares. The loan leg is treated the same way as a margin lending arrangement: Restricted Persons need prior Company approval to enter it or to transfer shares into a margin loan account, which the Company may condition (including as to margin-call sale terms), while a secured lender's enforcement sale on default is expressly excluded from the short-term dealing ban, blackout periods and the approval requirement altogether. The substance-over-form clause means the Company can look through the collar's structure to its economic effect when assessing compliance, and any collar entry, unwind or settlement must still avoid blackout periods (or obtain exceptional-circumstances approval) and pass the Front Page Test. Overall: workable for vested, unrestricted holdings with the required clearances and timing discipline; unavailable for unvested or holding-locked plan securities.

summary: For a Designated Person, a funded collar is workable if the loan is structured as an 'ordinary lending scenario' rather than a margin loan: clause 7.1 bans only margin lending arrangements and expressly carves out other secured funding using the shares as security, and the lender-disposal exemption in clause 6(g) likewise excludes margin loans but otherwise permits a secured lender's enforcement sale at any time, including during a Prohibited Period. The hedging ban (7.3(a)) only bites while the underlying remuneration securities are unvested or holding-locked; once vested and unlocked, the collar's put/call legs are third-party 'financial products' under clause 7.4 and are permitted only to the extent they fit a dealing type the policy already allows, in practice meaning dealt within an open trading window (post-results, post-AGM, prospectus, or cleansing-notice windows) after prior written notice to the Notification Officer and confirmation of no Inside Information, with post-trade confirmation to the Company Secretary within three business days. Outside a window, an exceptional-circumstances approval for severe hardship or a legal requirement is needed. Personnel who are not Designated Persons face none of the Part 7 restrictions at all and can deal, including in derivatives, within an open window without prior notification. The structure is achievable but turns entirely on characterising the loan as non-margin secured financing, since both the prohibition and its associated forced-sale exemption hinge on that label.

The real uncertainty is who grants that clearance for a DigiCo director or executive, since they sit in the 'LIT Persons' tier whose clearance process is meant to run through the manager's own trading policy (not in this document) even though s.6 also cross-refers to the EQT-specific Trading Request Procedure; the manager's own policy should be obtained before proceeding. Any entry, unwind or exercise must fall outside the half-year and full-year NTA/NAV blackout periods, any PDS/general-meeting/buy-back blackout, and while the individual holds no Inside Information. The Policy does not use a vesting concept, sets no minimum shareholding requirement or price-trigger guidance, and is silent on a lender's forced sale during a blackout period, so those risks are unaddressed rather than prohibited. If the arrangement is nonetheless treated as a dealing out of caution, the gate outside Closed/Blackout Periods is light: simple prior notice to the Company Secretary or Chairman and notice of completion, with no approval step; dealing timed within a Closed or Blackout Period instead needs the Chair's (or Audit & Risk Committee Chair's) written approval under the narrow Exceptional Circumstances process. The one hard stop that would apply regardless of how the structure is characterised is the absolute, undefined-length ban on short-term dealing in BKI securities, which has no listed exception, so tenor and unwind timing need care. Overall verdict: likely available given the Policy's silence on hedging and secured financing, subject only to notification (or Chair approval if timed inside a Prohibited Period) and avoiding any short-term dealing characterisation.

The loan leg is harder: margin lending arrangements, including transferring shares into a margin loan account or selling to satisfy a margin call, are banned outright with no exception under section 5.7.4, so a bank facility that is or resembles a margin lending arrangement cannot be cleared at all; a facility not structured as a margin loan is not addressed either way. Tenor should exceed three months, since the Policy names a forward contract as an example of short-term dealing that otherwise needs clearance from the section 5.5 approvers. summary: A funded collar appears possible under this policy, which is unusually thin: it contains no rule at all on margin lending, encumbrance, secured financing, or hedging, so the loan secured on the collared shares is not addressed or prohibited. The purchased put and written call would be caught only by the general insider trading prohibition, which expressly extends to 'division 3 financial products' (including derivatives) while the director or employee possesses undisclosed price sensitive information, and by the absolute closed period ban between financial year end and results release. Outside those constraints, any dealing requires standing notification to the Chairman, and if executed outside the Company's recommended four-week post-results trading window, prior notice to the Board which retains an unqualified veto. There is no clearance system, no defined validity period, no minimum shareholding requirement, and no distinction between vested and unvested securities. Given the policy's age (2010) and narrow scope, a funded collar is best timed within the four-week post-results window, confirmed with the Company Secretary as free of pending price sensitive announcements, and notified to the Chairman in advance.

summary: A funded collar is very difficult, though not per se impossible, under this policy. The hedging/derivatives bullet expressly bans put and call options, CFDs and similar arrangements that limit economic risk 'unless you have Written Clearance', but clearance may only be given where the trade is lawful, non-speculative, not seen as unfair, and justified by exceptional circumstances such as financial hardship or a court order -- criteria a routine portfolio-hedging collar is unlikely to satisfy. A separate, seemingly unqualified prohibition bans any arrangement 'designed to profit from a decrease in the share price', which likely captures the put leg regardless of clearance. The loan secured on the collared shares is not itself addressed by the policy, and a secured lender's eventual enforcement sale is expressly excluded from the policy's application altogether. Any clearance obtained is void if the person holds inside information, and no Restricted Period dealing is possible without it. In practice, a funded collar would need Written Clearance from the applicable Authorised Officer (CEO, two directors, or two non-executive directors/NED-plus-CEO-or-CFO depending on tier) on genuinely exceptional grounds, executed outside a Restricted Period and free of inside information, with residual risk around the unwaivable profit-from-decline bullet.

For Designated Persons outside the Directors/Executives tier, the margin loan ban does not apply and financing is only addressed via a disclosure question on the Personal Trading Approval Form, but the same 4.8(b) derivatives-dealing ban still applies. On its face, neither the purchased put and written call nor a loan secured on the collared shares is prohibited by the Policy's express terms. The shares themselves remain subject to two annual blackout periods (1 July to full-year results, and 1 January to half-year results) for any actual sale or transfer needed to establish, unwind or settle the structure, during which Directors, Senior Managers and Other Employees need sole-discretion clearance from the Chairman, Audit Committee Chairman or CEO respectively (or can rely on the narrow Exceptional Circumstances hardship/court-order gateway); outside a blackout period, Directors and Senior Managers must simply notify the appropriate officer, and Other Employees need not do even that. summary: A funded collar with a bank is not achievable under this policy.
